correctness.rationale: The first-column perfect-matching dichotomy yields two contractible subcomplexes with exact intersection X(n-2). The blockwise subcomplex has the same two-cone pushout pattern. The map of pushout diagrams is an ordinary homotopy equivalence by induction and the CW gluing theorem. Each block has two disjoint edge simplices, each equivariantly retractable to its barycenter; their join is a sphere, preserving the row/column group action. Row exchange preserves the two component labels in each block; reversal permutes all k factors in reverse order, giving sign (-1)^{k(k-1)/2} on the degree-(k-1) integral join generator. Rational finite-group coinvariants give the quotient conclusion. All quantifiers include k=1, which is the exact base. Independent finite face/Lefschetz computations cover n=2,4,6,8,10 and verify mod-two Betti ranks through n=8. No equivariant homotopy inverse or integral quotient homology is asserted.

originality.rationale: Theorem 3.3 of Chandrakar--Singh already proves the nonequivariant sphere homotopy type and is credited. The inspected theorem, its proof, and its appendix do not state an invariant blockwise homology-detecting sphere, integral row-swap/column-reversal characters, or the rational quotient dichotomy. Those statements do not follow from the unmarked homotopy type alone: the same sphere can support multiple one-dimensional symmetry characters. The closest indexed ladder results concern total-cut, ordinary matching, or periodic-ladder complexes rather than this perfect-matching complex.

value.rationale: The complete integral character for the natural full geometric symmetry group of all non-square even ladders, together with an invariant geometric sphere carrying the generator, resolves a natural equivariant refinement of a previously known nonequivariant classification. The alternating reversal orientation gives a sharp periodic rational quotient-homology dichotomy for the entire infinite family. This is a structural and topologically motivated classification, not a single small calculation or merely another proof of the known sphere type.
